matched_finding.subcategory: iatrogenic change sign ambiguity in Table 1
matched_finding.description: Table 1 reports the iatrogenic change in 'Desire to die (0-10)' as 0.20 (positive, implying an increase from pre to post session). However, the Results text reports 'desire to die from pre (M=0.82, SD=1.10) to post (M=0.61, SD=0.90) significantly decreased slightly, t(32)=2.23, p=.033.' The correct change score is −0.21 (a decrease). The positive value in Table 1 is therefore either a sign error or represents an absolute magnitude without direction, creating a potentially misleading impression that suicidal ideation increased during the study session. The t-test statistic and p-value indicate a significant decrease, consistent with the text but not the table value.
matched_finding.quote: Iatrogenic – change pre to post | Desire to die (0-10) | 0.20

ground_truth.original_snippet: A sample of 33 participants with at least one reported past suicide attempt were recruited from the University of Virginia Psychology Department’s participant pool and from the Charlottesville community.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: A sample of 33 participants with at least one reported past suicide attempt were recruited from the Charlottesville community.

matched_finding.description: The sample is 84.8% female, 60.6% Caucasian, mean age 20.4 years, 94% with 'some college' education, and recruited from a university participant pool. This demographic profile is highly unrepresentative of the broader population of suicide attempters. Suicide attempt rates and methods, communication patterns, and text messaging behavior differ substantially by gender, age, education, and race/ethnicity. Males are four times more likely to die by suicide yet represent only ~15% of the sample. The paper acknowledges the gender-completion discrepancy in limitations but does not adequately flag that these demographic features may fundamentally alter the generalizability of all findings—including the specific language features identified.
matched_finding.quote: Most of the participants were female, White, and college-aged.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Social support vs social engagement — subtle construct distinction
ground_truth.original_snippet: In theory, social support should combat such feelings and increase feelings of connectedness.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: In theory, social engagement should combat such feelings and increase feelings of connectedness.
ground_truth.description: Changed 'social support' (perceived caring) to 'social engagement' (behavioral frequency) — collapses theory-operationalization gap that's a real limitation; message volume is weak proxy for perceived support

matched_finding.subcategory: social engagement operationalization does not match interpersonal theory constructs
matched_finding.description: The interpersonal theory of suicide (Joiner, 2005; Van Orden et al., 2010) specifies two distinct constructs: thwarted belongingness (feeling disconnected from others) and perceived burdensomeness (feeling like a burden). The study operationalizes social engagement as the ratio of sent to received text messages and counts of outgoing/incoming messages. Message frequency and direction do not constitute valid operationalizations of either thwarted belongingness or perceived burdensomeness—a person could send many messages while feeling profoundly disconnected, or could feel burdened without reducing outgoing communication. The operationalization is also atheoretical with respect to which direction changes should occur: the hypothesized decrease in outgoing messages is not clearly derivable from the theory.
matched_finding.quote: we tested whether suicide attempters demonstrated greater signs of disengagement from and burdensomeness on their social support networks prior to suicide attempts compared to other episodes by examining patterns in outgoing vs. incoming messages.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: No random slopes with marginal p-values — must know Barr et al recommendations
ground_truth.original_snippet: Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, only a by-participant slope of episode type was included in the final model.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, no random slopes were included in the final model.
ground_truth.description: Removed all random slopes (kept only intercepts) — fails to account for participant variability in episode effects; inflates Type I error per Barr et al (2013); key p-values near .05 may become false positives

matched_finding.subcategory: random effects convergence failures inadequately described
matched_finding.description: The Methods state that a maximal random effects model was planned, including random slopes for episode type, day, and their interaction by participant. The authors then note 'Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, only a by-participant slope of episode type was included in the final model.' This is a significant deviation from the stated analytic plan, but it is not reported which specific random slopes were dropped, whether different models were tested, or whether the simplification was applied identically across all outcome variables. Non-convergence can indicate model misspecification beyond just overfitting, and the consequences for inference depend on which slopes were dropped.
matched_finding.quote: Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, only a by-participant slope of episode type was included in the final model.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Claims all 27 had attempt data but only 15 did — must check if 27=27 makes sense given design
ground_truth.original_snippet: Among these 27 participants, 15 had data from at least one reported suicide attempt; the other 12 participants contributed data from non-suicide attempt episodes and were still included in the analyses.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: Among these 27 participants, all had data from at least one reported suicide attempt.
ground_truth.description: Concealed that only 15/27 (56%) had attempt SMS data — hides selection bias in who contributes to the critical attempt vs non-attempt comparisons

matched_finding.subcategory: severe episode-level missing data with systematic bias
matched_finding.description: Only 134 of 293 collected episodes (46%) contained any SMS data, meaning 54% of episodes provided no data. More critically, only 15 of 33 participants had SMS data from at least one suicide attempt episode—the central comparison condition of the study. The remaining 12 participants with any data contributed exclusively to non-attempt episode comparisons. This means the primary within-subjects comparison (attempt vs. other episodes) is effectively based on a subset of 15 participants, yet the stated N is 33. The authors acknowledge this but claim mixed-effects models 'handle missing data,' which addresses statistical estimation but does not resolve the underlying selection bias: participants lacking attempt SMS data may differ systematically (e.g., older attempts, phone changes, encryption use) in ways related to the constructs studied.
matched_finding.quote: Among these 27 participants, 15 had data from at least one reported suicide attempt; the other 12 participants contributed data from non-suicide attempt episodes and were still included in the analyses.
